cues.text: Hello everyone, and welcome back!
Today is a really exciting one: Lecture ten, Multimodal Large Language Models.
So far in this course, our models could only read text.
Today, we teach them to see, to hear, and even to act in the world.
Let's go!
Before we start the technical part, let me share a piece of good news from our own campus.
This is a post from our president, Professor Yangsheng Xu.
A PhD student from our university co-founded a medical imaging startup called Cognita, and served as its CTO.
And about a year ago, Cognita was acquired by Mosaic Clinical Technologies, for nearly one hundred million US dollars!
So what did they build? Vision-language models for radiology.
Compared with radiologists working alone, their AI reduced major diagnostic errors by up to four times, and saved up to seventy-six percent of reading time.
Think about it: a model that looks at a medical image, and writes the report like a doctor.
That is exactly the kind of multimodal model we are going to study today.
So, join the journey on multimodal LLMs for society!
Here is our roadmap for today.
We start with the foundations: why multimodality matters, and how vision meets language, with CLIP and Flamingo.
Then we build multimodal LLMs ourselves: the architecture, and how to train them.
And then we go beyond images: speech language models, generation and world simulators, embodied agents, and 3D.
Now look at the bottom of the slide.
The story of today is simple: see, talk, hear and speak, imagine, act, and finally, understand space.
Six verbs. That is what a truly multimodal AI should be able to do.
Okay! Part one: why multimodality?
Think about how you are experiencing this lecture right now.
You see me, you hear my voice, you read the slides, all at the same time.
Text alone is a very narrow window onto a world full of images, sound, and motion.
Here is one of my favorite examples. Even listening is multimodal!
Look at this traditional Chinese character, ting, which means: to listen.
Of course, it contains an ear.
But it also contains an eye, and a heart.
So thousands of years ago, the people who created this character already knew: real listening uses your ears, your eyes, and your heart.
And modern cognitive science agrees. The brain combines sound, vision, and language, all at once.
If humans understand the world this way, our AI should too.
And that is exactly why we need multimodal large language models.
So what exactly do we mean by multimodality? Let's start with what it looks like in practice.
On the left, you see all the behaviors and signals that humans actually produce when they communicate.
Language, of course: words, syntax, pragmatics.
But also acoustic signals like intonation and laughter, and visual signals like gestures, eye gaze, and facial expressions.
And even touch, physiological signals like heart activity, and mobile sensors like GPS and accelerometers.
Text is just one small box in this big picture!
Now look at the right: a multimodal AI model for healthcare.
It takes surgical images, a text note like: the patient developed heart failure, and photos with questions.
All of them become tokens, get concatenated into one input, and go into a single multitask model.
So a user can ask: what caused this rash? And the AI answers: this is probably an allergic reaction.
Now let's be a bit more precise. Here's the definition.
A modality is the way in which something is expressed or perceived.
And here's a nice way to think about it: modalities live on a spectrum.
On the left, raw modalities, closest to the sensor, like the speech signal or a raw image.
As we move right, things get more abstract: language, and detected objects.
And at the far right, abstract modalities like sentiment intensity or object categories, farthest from the sensor.
Notice where language sits: it is already a compressed, processed version of the world.
Here's a fun fact about the word itself. Multimodal, as an adjective, means having several modes, modalities, or maxima.
In statistics, a multimodal distribution is one with several peaks, just like the 3D plot on the right.
But in this course, we care about a different meaning.
For us in NLP, multimodal means text plus one or more other modalities: images, speech, audio, even smell.
And today, we will mostly focus on images as the other modality.
Okay, so why should we care? There is a whole range of very good reasons.
First, faithfulness. Human experience is multimodal: we see, hear, smell, taste, and touch.
Second, it is practical. The internet and so many real applications are full of images, videos, and audio.
Third, data efficiency and availability.
Multimodal data is rich and high bandwidth.
Yann LeCun even called language an imperfect, incomplete, and low-bandwidth serialization protocol for the internal data structures we call thoughts.
So maybe learning from richer signals is simply better for learning.
And scaling: more data is better, but we are running out of high-quality text data.
Images and videos are the next huge reservoir.
That's why multimodality is one of the main frontiers of the foundation model revolution.
There are so many amazing multimodal systems today, so which ones should we study first?
We start with two early milestones: CLIP from two thousand twenty-one, and Flamingo from two thousand twenty-two.
They are important, and their public details are clear, which makes them perfect for learning.
CLIP was the first model that could generalize to many image classification tasks with zero-shot and few-shot learning.
Flamingo was not the first model to generate open-ended responses about images.
But its performance was so strong that some people called it the GPT-3 moment of the multimodal domain.
And building on them, we arrive at today's multimodal LLMs.
So how do we actually connect vision and language? Let's start with CLIP.
Part two: connecting vision and language.
Two early ideas shaped every multimodal LLM you will see today.
First, CLIP teaches images and text to live in the same space.
Then Flamingo lets a language model actually talk about images. Let's dive in!
Let's start with CLIP.
Here's the key idea: map images into the text space, using a contrastive objective.
Simple, scalable, and still one of the best practices for aligning vision with language.
CLIP stands for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, from OpenAI in two thousand twenty-one.
It combines two ingredients: natural language supervision, and contrastive learning.
Together, they let CLIP scale up its data and make training much more efficient.
Now look at what this buys us on the right: zero-shot image classification.
Show CLIP a photo of food, and it ranks guacamole first out of one hundred and one labels, with ninety point one percent.
Show it an airplane, and again it picks the right answer, with eighty-nine percent.
Notice the labels are just sentences, like a photo of a guacamole, a type of food.
And nobody trained it on these datasets! So why and how do these two techniques work? Let's see.
Here is CLIP's high-level architecture. It has two towers.
A piece of text, like happy hippie hamster, goes into a text encoder and becomes a text embedding.
And the picture of the hamster goes into an image encoder and becomes an image embedding.
But these two embeddings have different sizes, so they live in different worlds.
So each one is multiplied by a projection matrix, landing in one shared multimodal embedding space.
There, we simply compute a cosine similarity score between text and image.
Both encoders and both projection matrices are trained jointly, from scratch.
The goal: high similarity for the right image-text pairs, low similarity for the wrong ones. That is contrastive learning.
But to train this, you need a lot of image-text pairs. Where do they come from?
For many years, image models were trained on manually annotated datasets, like ImageNet and MS COCO.
But manual annotation is slow and expensive. It simply does not scale.
The CLIP authors found no existing dataset big enough and clean enough, so they built their own: four hundred million image-text pairs.
Step one: build a list of five hundred thousand queries, from common words, bigrams, and popular Wikipedia titles.
Step two: find images matching these queries. The paper says not via search engines, so most likely an internal web crawl.
Step three, and this is the clever part: pair each image with the text that naturally appears next to it, like captions or comments.
Why not just the query? Because a query is too short to really describe the image.
So the internet itself becomes the annotator, for free!
What does such web data look like? Here is a concrete example, a Wikipedia page about Half Dome.
One page gives you many kinds of text for free: the page title, and the page description.
And here is the image, with its own reference description right below it.
This is the idea behind WIT, the Wikipedia-based Image Text dataset.
Every image comes with natural, human-written language around it. No extra labeling needed.
And it gets even bigger. Meet LAION-5B, an open dataset with billions of image-text pairs.
Each sample has an image URL, covering millions of domains, and a caption text.
Look at the similarity column: the cosine between image and text embeddings, computed with CLIP itself.
So CLIP is now used to clean the data for the next generation of models. Nice loop, right?
There are also safety signals: the probability of a watermark, and the probability of unsafe content.
The data comes in three subsets: English, multilingual, and no detected language.
And notice the captions are short: on average sixty-seven, fifty-two, and forty-six.
Web text is short and noisy, but there is a huge amount of it.
Here is a snapshot of image datasets that exist today.
The top half are open-source image-text datasets.
LAION-5B alone has five billion image-text pairs, about two hundred forty terabytes compressed.
Then there are interleaved web documents like OBELICS and MMC4, and MINT-1T with two point six billion pairs.
The bottom half are commercial or domain datasets: art, photography, travel notes, recipes, and encyclopedias of species and plants.
The lesson: data is the fuel, and the community has collected a lot of it since CLIP.
Now, given all this data, what should the training objective be?
Let's compare two ways to do image classification: discriminative and generative.
Both start from a predetermined list of classes, like dog, cat, and so on.
A classifier outputs one probability distribution, and picks a single class. Here, cat.
A language model does the same thing, but again and again: it outputs a sequence of classes.
So you get cat, and, dog, and so on.
Each generated class is a token, and the list of classes is simply the vocabulary.
So the generative way is much more flexible. Then why didn't CLIP just generate captions?
Here's the problem. Look at these two images.
Each one has five different human captions, and all of them are correct!
Several men in hard hats, or three men on a large rig. Same picture, very different words.
So the texts for an image are diverse.
The CLIP authors found that a language model objective made training difficult.
Their hypothesis: the model is forced to predict the exact text for each image, while many texts could fit, like alt-text, captions, or comments.
That is a much harder task than it needs to be. So how do we fix it?
The answer is contrastive learning.
Instead of predicting the exact text, CLIP only predicts whether a text is more likely to go with an image than other texts.
Take a batch of N image-text pairs. We get N image embeddings, V, and N text embeddings, L.
Now compute the cosine similarity for all N squared possible pairings.
Only N of them are correct. Push those scores up, and push the other N squared minus N scores down.
And for CLIP, N is thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-eight!
That means every image is contrasted against more than thirty thousand texts in one step. Huge batches give lots of negatives.
Here is the famous CLIP figure, which puts everything together.
Part one, contrastive pre-training. Texts go through the text encoder, images go through the image encoder.
This gives a grid of all image-text dot products.
The blue diagonal holds the correct pairs. Training pushes them up, and everything off the diagonal down.
Part two: to build a classifier, take your label names, like plane, car, dog, and bird.
Put each label into a prompt, a photo of a blank, and encode it with the text encoder.
Part three: encode a new image, and compare it against all those label embeddings.
The best match wins: a photo of a dog.
Notice what just happened. The text encoder became a classifier, with zero training examples. That is zero-shot!
So how good is zero-shot CLIP?
This chart compares zero-shot CLIP against a linear probe trained on ResNet-50 features, across twenty-seven datasets.
Green means CLIP wins. On StanfordCars it gains twenty-eight point nine points, and on Food101, twenty-two point five.
Even on ImageNet it wins, by one point nine, without seeing a single ImageNet training label.
In total, it wins on sixteen of these twenty-seven datasets.
Blue means CLIP loses, on specialized tasks like satellite images in EuroSAT, distance estimation in KITTI, or digits in MNIST.
Takeaway: for many classification tasks, CLIP is still a strong out-of-the-box baseline, used as-is or fine-tuned.
A second application: text-based image retrieval.
CLIP's training is basically retrieval in disguise: match images to texts, and texts to images.
The paper says it shows significant promise for image search, but admits it is noticeably below the state of the art there.
Still, people use it. The clip-retrieval package is a good example.
First, embed all your images with CLIP and store them in a vector database.
Then embed the text query, and look up the images whose embeddings are closest to it.
Simple, fast, and it works with any words you like.
And a third application: image generation.
Start from a prompt: a corgi playing a flame throwing trumpet.
Above the dotted line is CLIP training: the text encoder and image encoder are aligned by the CLIP objective.
Below the line, a prior turns the text embedding into a CLIP image embedding.
Then a decoder turns that image embedding into an actual picture.
This is the design behind DALL-E 2. CLIP's shared space becomes the bridge from words to pixels.
But notice what CLIP itself cannot do: it can match and rank, but it cannot write a single word about an image.
So how do we get a language model to look at images and generate text? That brings us to Flamingo.
Now, the second piece of early work: Flamingo.
CLIP could match images and text, but it could not say a single word about an image.
Flamingo changes that: it lets a generative language model actually talk about images, and that is the dawn of large multimodal models.
So what is Flamingo, in one line?
In a reductive view, Flamingo equals CLIP plus an autoregressive language model.
Here's the key difference: by adding a decoder language model, Flamingo can generate text responses, which CLIP simply cannot do.
And the image encoder and the language model interact through attention.
Look at these conversations. You can ask about a dog: what breed is it, is it running?
You can ask which city a street sign is in, play the Stroop color test, or compare a triangle with a hexagon.
In every case, Flamingo generates text conditioned on both the text and the images, in a multi-turn dialogue.
That is a huge step beyond retrieval. So how is it built? Let's open the box.
Here is the high-level architecture of Flamingo.
The input is interleaved visual and text data, like a picture of a dog, some text, then a picture of a cat, then more text.
Each image goes through a vision encoder, which is pretrained and frozen; see the little snowflake.
Then a Perceiver Resampler, trained from scratch, turns the visual features into a small set of visual tokens.
On the right, the text is processed, with special image tags marking where each picture appears.
The language model blocks are frozen, and between them we insert new GATED XATTN-DENSE layers that look at the visual tokens.
And the output is just text: a very serious cat.
So, two parts: a CLIP-like vision encoder trained contrastively, whose text encoder is then thrown away.
And a Chinchilla language model, extended with two new components: the Perceiver Resampler and the gated cross-attention layers.
Before we zoom into those components, let's look at what data feeds this model.
Flamingo used four datasets: two image-text pair datasets, one video-text pair dataset, and one interleaved image and text dataset.
Image-text pairs are what we saw with CLIP: a picture and its caption.
Video-text pairs add time, like a kid doing a kickflip.
And the new one is M3W, the MultiModal MassiveWeb dataset: real webpages where images and text are mixed together.
Look at the table: M3W has forty-three million webpages, and from each page they sample two hundred fifty-six tokens with up to five images.
ALIGN has one point eight billion pairs with short alt-texts, and LTIP has three hundred twelve million pairs with longer descriptions.
VTP has twenty-seven million short videos, about twenty-two seconds each.
Notice the training weights: the interleaved M3W data gets weight one point zero, much more than the others.
Why does that matter? Interleaved data teaches the model to read several images and texts in one sequence, which is exactly what few-shot prompting needs.
Now the language model itself.
Flamingo uses Chinchilla, and the pretrained Chinchilla layers are kept frozen.
A traditional language model predicts the next text token from the preceding text tokens.
Flamingo predicts the next text token from both the preceding text and the visual tokens.
So the images become part of the context, but the model still only outputs text.
But wait: how do we turn images into a neat set of visual tokens? That's the Perceiver Resampler.
Here's the problem: the visual input can be a single image or a whole video.
So the vision encoder produces a variable number of features, one grid per frame.
We add time embeddings for each frame, and flatten everything into one long sequence of features.
Now here's the trick: a small set of learned latent queries.
These latents act as the queries, and the visual features act as keys and values in attention, followed by a feed-forward layer.
Because the number of queries is fixed, the output size is fixed too: always sixty-four visual tokens, no matter how long the video is.
The code on the right is short: for each layer, attention, then feed-forward, both with residual connections.
Think of it as a compressor that summarizes any visual input into a fixed budget of tokens for the language model.
So how does the frozen language model actually look at these visual tokens? With GATED XATTN-DENSE layers.
These new layers are inserted between the existing, frozen LM layers.
Zoom in: first comes cross-attention, where the queries come from the language, and the keys and values come from the vision features.
Then a dense feed-forward layer, and after that the original frozen self-attention and feed-forward layers.
Here's the clever part: each new branch is multiplied by tanh of a gate parameter, alpha, which is initialized at zero.
Tanh of zero is zero, so at the start the language model behaves exactly like the original Chinchilla.
Then, during training, the gates slowly open and visual information flows in, which keeps training stable.
And it matters: according to the ablation quoted here, without this design the overall score drops by four point two percent.
Now, what is the training objective? Good news: it's our old friend, the autoregressive language modeling loss.
Flamingo computes the likelihood of the text y, conditioned on the interleaved images and videos x.
It's a product over tokens: each text token depends on the previous text tokens and on the images that came before it.
The training loss is a weighted sum of negative log-likelihoods across all four datasets.
And lambda m is the weight of dataset m, exactly the training weights we saw in the data table.
So no new magic in the loss. All the novelty is in the architecture and the data.
One practical note: Flamingo itself was never open-sourced.
But the community built open replications, like IDEFICS from Hugging Face, and OpenFlamingo from mlfoundations.
If you want to play with a Flamingo-style model in your project, these are great starting points.
Let's wrap up this part by putting CLIP and Flamingo side by side.
Data: CLIP used four hundred million image-text pairs, while Flamingo mixed four datasets, including interleaved webpages.
Both train a vision encoder with the same contrastive objective; Flamingo uses an NFNet, and then freezes it.
And Flamingo's text encoder, a BERT, is used only for that contrastive step and then discarded.
But look at the last row: CLIP has no language model at all.
Flamingo adds a frozen Chinchilla, a Perceiver Resampler with sixty-four visual tokens, and gated cross-attention layers trained from scratch.
That is the real leap: from matching images and text, to generating language about images.
So, frozen vision encoder, a connector, and a powerful language model: keep this recipe in mind.
Because next, we'll see how modern multimodal LLMs are built on exactly this idea. Let's go!
Welcome to Part three: the architecture of multimodal LLMs.
We just saw how CLIP aligns images with text, and how Flamingo lets a language model look at images.
Now here is the big recipe: keep language as the pivot, encode the other modalities, project them into the LLM's token space, and let the LLM reason.
Let's see how this is actually built!
First, a quick question: why build multimodal LLMs at all?
Welcome to the era of large language models.
Large language models really improved cognition-level abilities, like reasoning and planning.
But on their own, they only read and write text, so they cannot directly see the world. That is the gap we want to close.
So what does a multimodal LLM look like in action? Here is a chat with LLaVA.
The user uploads a screenshot and asks: what is written, and who could be interested in this content?
Look at the answer.
The model describes the city skyline and the sunset, and it reads the text: recent advances in vision foundation models.
Then it goes one step further and reasons that researchers in computer vision and AI might care, and that it is probably a conference event.
So it sees, it reads, and it reasons, all in one conversation.
Here is the preliminary idea behind almost all of these systems.
Emergent phenomena have already shown up extensively in language-based LLMs.
These models now have very powerful semantic understanding capabilities.
And that tells us something deep: language is a crucial modality for carrying intelligence.
So if the intelligence already lives in language, why not build on top of it?
And that is exactly what the field did.
Nearly all current multimodal LLMs use a language-based LLM as the core decision-making module, the brain, or the central processor.
Then we add external modules for the non-textual modalities.
Look at the picture: visual, video, and 3D on the left, smell, sound, and touch on the right, all flowing into language in the middle.
Language is the pivot, the hub that everything connects to.
Why bother? It extends the capability boundary, it is the next milestone toward more advanced intelligence, and it opens up many more applications.
But wait. Is language really the right pivot for intelligence? Let's pause on a little debate.
Here is Noam Chomsky.
He argues that the purpose of language is not only communication; it is also used to express and clarify thought, for play, and to gain understanding.
In his view, there is no reason to give either mode a privileged status.
On the other hand, a recent perspective paper in Nature argues that language is primarily a tool for communication rather than thought.
So the question is still open. But in practice, language has turned out to be an extremely useful hub for today's models.
Now, given language as the pivot, there are two ways to connect the other modalities. Let's look at type one.
Type one: the LLM as a discrete scheduler, or controller.
Here the LLM receives textual signals, and sends out textual commands to call downstream modules.
Follow the diagram: the user sends text to the LLM, and the LLM sends text to a set of downstream tools.
The results then come back to the user.
Here's the key feature: every message in the system, from encoder to LLM, or from LLM to tools, is pure text.
The LLM never sees the pixels. It only reads and writes words.
Many well-known systems follow this design.
Visual-ChatGPT, HuggingGPT, MM-REACT, ViperGPT, AudioGPT, and LLaVA-Plus, to name a few.
They all share the same loop: user, LLM, tools, and back to the user.
Let's look at two of them in more detail.
On the left is Visual ChatGPT.
The user asks for something complex, like generating a red flower from the depth of an image, and then making it a cartoon.
A prompt manager lets ChatGPT call visual foundation models like BLIP, Stable Diffusion, and ControlNet, step by step.
On the right is HuggingGPT, where the LLM is the controller and Hugging Face models are the tools.
It goes through four stages: task planning, model selection, task execution, and response generation.
The good news: it is quick to build, with no training, and you can flexibly plug in many tools.
The bad news: everything is squeezed through text, so information gets lost. Text becomes the bottleneck.
Can a caption really capture every detail of an image? Of course not. So we need something better.
That brings us to type two: the LLM as a joint part of the system.
More than ninety percent of multimodal LLMs belong to this category.
It has a higher upper bound, because everything is integrated into one unified model.
Look at the pipeline: a modality encoder turns images, audio, or video into features.
A connector maps those features into tokens the LLM can read, right next to the text tokens.
The LLM reasons over all of them, and an optional generator can even produce images, audio, or video.
At the bottom, you see three common connectors: a simple MLP, a Q-Former with learnable queries, and cross-attention inside the LLM.
Notice the last one: that is exactly the Flamingo style you saw earlier.
Now let's open the box and look at real architectures.
We will walk through LLaVA, Qwen-VL, CogVLM, and Fuyu, and then the newest native and unified models.
Watch for one question every time: how does the image get into the LLM?
Let's start with LLaVA, the Large Language-and-Vision Assistant. It is beautifully simple.
The image goes into a vision encoder, which gives visual features Z v.
Then a projection matrix W maps them into H v, visual tokens in the same space as the word embeddings.
These visual tokens sit right next to the language instruction tokens, H q.
The language model reads them all and generates the response.
Training has two stages.
Stage one is feature alignment: only the projection matrix is updated, using a subset of CC3M.
Stage two is end-to-end fine-tuning: both the projection and the LLM are updated, on visual chat data and Science QA.
One linear layer as the bridge, and it works surprisingly well!
Next, Qwen-VL from Alibaba.
Instead of a plain projection, it uses a cross-attention module with learnable query embeddings to compress the ViT features.
Now watch the fire and snowflake icons: fire means trainable, snowflake means frozen.
Stage one is pretraining on image-text pairs at low resolution, with the LLM frozen.
Stage two is multi-task pretraining with high resolution and interleaved vision-language data, and now everything is trained.
Stage three is supervised fine-tuning on chat data, with the ViT frozen.
So the lesson is: carefully choose what to train, and when.
Now CogVLM, which takes a deeper approach.
On the left, the input looks familiar: a ViT encoder plus an MLP adapter for the image, and word embeddings for the text.
The two sequences are concatenated and fed into the language model.
But look at the right side: this is the visual expert.
Inside every Transformer block, image features get their own QKV matrix and their own FFN, separate from the text.
Only the purple parts are trainable, so the original language model stays untouched.
This gives vision deep fusion at every layer, without hurting the language ability.
And here is the most minimal design of all: Fuyu.
There is no separate vision encoder at all!
The input image is cut into patches, and each patch goes through a simple linear projection.
These patch embeddings go straight into the Transformer decoder, just like word tokens.
Notice the newline tokens: they mark the end of each row of patches, so the model knows the image layout.
Then the text follows, and the model says: this is a Fuyu persimmon.
One decoder, images and text treated almost the same way.
Now the newest trend: a paradigm shift from modular to native multimodal models.
GPT-4o from OpenAI, two thousand twenty-four, is an omni-model: text, image, audio, and video, natively, in one end-to-end architecture.
Gemini 2.0 from Google is native multimodal from the ground up, not CLIP plus LLM stitching.
The key advantage? It removes the information bottleneck between the vision encoder and the LLM.
And it enables real-time interaction, with voice, vision, and text all at once.
The trend keeps going: Meta's Muse Spark, and Qwen3.5 as native multimodal agents.
What about the open-source world? It is moving very fast too.
Qwen2.5-VL from Alibaba brings dynamic resolution, video understanding, and agent capabilities.
InternVL2.5 from Shanghai AI Lab scales up to seventy-eight billion parameters, with strong OCR and document understanding.
DeepSeek-VL2 uses a mixture-of-experts architecture for efficient multimodal reasoning.
LLaVA-OneVision is one unified model for single images, video, and multi-image tasks.
And MiniCPM-V 2.6 is edge-efficient, rivaling GPT-4V on mobile devices.
So you can build on strong open models today, even on your own phone.
Finally, can one model both understand images and generate them? That is the goal of unified models.
Janus-Pro from DeepSeek decouples visual encoding for understanding and for generation, but keeps one unified Transformer backbone.
Emu3 from BAAI does next-token prediction for text, image, and video, all as discrete tokens, and it was published in Nature.
Chameleon from Meta is an early-fusion, token-based multimodal model.
Here's the key insight: understanding needs semantic features, while generation needs low-level detail, so they may want different encoders.
Our own work, ShareGPT-4o-Image, also explores this direction, and we will come back to it later in the lecture.
Notice how everything we saw today starts from the same place: how do we turn pixels into something the LLM can use?
So let's zoom in on that first component: the visual encoder, or tokenizer.
Here it is: the part that turns pixels into something a language model can digest.
Should we use a continuous visual encoder, or a tokenizer that turns images into discrete tokens, just like words?
Let's look at both options.
Let's start with the most common choice: CLIP-ViT, the vision transformer trained with CLIP.
Why is it so popular? Because CLIP was trained to match images with text, so its image features already live close to the text space.
That makes connecting it to a language model much easier.
It also scales well: more parameters and more data give you better features.
Look at this chart: zero-shot accuracy against model size, on a log scale.
As the CLIP models get bigger, the accuracy keeps going up.
And a newer option, SigLIP, is gaining popularity, because it is smaller and stronger.
It replaces CLIP's softmax contrastive loss with a simple sigmoid loss on each image-text pair.
But these pretrained ViTs have a real limitation.
They take a fixed, low-resolution, square input: two twenty-four by two twenty-four, or three thirty-six by three thirty-six pixels.
Look at this street photo.
Squeeze it into a tiny thumbnail, blow it back up, and everything gets blurry.
Can you read the shop signs? I can't, and neither can the model.
Low resolution encoding misses the fine-grained visual details.
So high-resolution perception is essential, especially for OCR, reading text in images, documents and charts.
So how do we fix it?
The popular answer is simple: slice the image.
Take a high-resolution image, and split it into a grid of tiles, here two by two.
Each tile is encoded separately by the same visual encoder, at the resolution it was trained on.
